Poverty
POV-er-tee
n.
From Old French poverte, from Latin paupertas (poverty), from pauper (poor). Renders the Hebrew rīsh, rēsh, “poverty,” and the Greek ptōcheia, “destitution, beggary.”

📖 Biblical Definition

Poverty in Scripture is treated in two registers, material and spiritual, and the Bible refuses to collapse either into the other. Material poverty is the actual lack of the goods necessary for life—food, clothing, shelter, the means of provision—and Scripture addresses it pastorally with sustained seriousness: the law commanded gleaning and the year of jubilee, the prophets thundered against the oppression of the poor, the wisdom literature counseled both the diligence that ordinarily prevents poverty and the generosity that relieves it, the apostles gathered collections for the poor saints at Jerusalem, and Christ Himself stood for the poor and preached the gospel to them as the credential of His mission. The biblical disposition toward the materially poor is mercy, justice, and active relief; the biblical warnings to the church are sharp against any neglect (whoso hath this world’s good, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him?). Spiritual poverty—poverty of spirit—is the deeper biblical category, and it is the opening Beatitude: Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Spiritual poverty is the inward state of the soul that knows itself bankrupt before God, has no righteousness of its own to plead, is empty of self-righteousness and self-sufficiency, and casts itself entirely upon the grace of God in Christ. It is the very opposite of the Laodicean self-assessment (I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing) and the precondition of every saving response to the gospel: the soul that does not feel its poverty cannot receive the riches of Christ. The two poverties intersect deeply but are not identical. The materially rich may be spiritually poor (Abraham, Joseph, David), and the materially poor may be spiritually rich (the Macedonian saints whose deep poverty abounded unto the riches of their liberality); but Scripture warns that material wealth disposes the heart toward spiritual self-sufficiency in a way that material poverty does not (how hardly shall they that have riches enter into the kingdom of God!), and that the poor have therefore often heard the gospel more gladly than the rich precisely because their material situation has not insulated them against the diagnosis the gospel makes. The Christ who for our sakes became poor that we through His poverty might be rich (2 Cor 8:9) sums up the doctrine in His own person: the divine emptying that became the church’s eternal riches.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines POVERTY as destitution of property; indigence; want of convenient means of subsistence; figuratively, want of spirit; meanness; defect or deficiency.

expand to see more

POVERTY, n. — 1. Destitution of property; indigence; want of convenient means of subsistence. 2. Barrenness of sentiment or ornament; defect; as, the poverty of a composition. 3. Want; defect; as, the poverty of language. 4. In scripture, that humble state of mind that is sensible of the want of righteousness in oneself, and looks to Christ for it (Matt 5:3).

📖 Key Scripture

Matthew 5:3 — "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven."

2 Corinthians 8:9 — "For ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich."

Revelation 3:17 — "Because thou sayest, I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing; and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked."

2 Corinthians 8:2 — "How that in a great trial of affliction the abundance of their joy and their deep poverty abounded unto the riches of their liberality."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The biblical doctrine of poverty is corrupted by the prosperity gospel that treats material poverty as a sign of insufficient faith and material wealth as the credential of God’s favor—and by the inverse romanticization of poverty in certain progressive traditions that treats material poverty itself as virtue and obscures the deeper biblical category of poverty of spirit.

expand to see more

The prosperity gospel corrupts the biblical doctrine of poverty by reading material wealth as the credential of God’s favor and material poverty as a sign of insufficient faith. The Scripture refuses both ends of this read. The materially poor include Christ Himself (who had no place to lay His head), the apostles (who left all to follow Him and ended their lives in want and martyrdom), the saints of Hebrews 11 (who wandered in deserts and mountains, of whom the world was not worthy), and the Macedonian churches whose deep poverty abounded unto the riches of their liberality. The materially rich include Abraham, Job, Joseph, David, Solomon, Joseph of Arimathea, and Lydia. Material condition is not the measure of God’s favor; the prosperity gospel’s confusion of the two leaves the materially poor saint inappropriately ashamed and the materially comfortable sinner inappropriately confident, and obscures the much more serious diagnostic Scripture actually makes: the danger of riches to the soul precisely because they incline the heart toward the spiritual self-sufficiency that bars the kingdom.

The opposite corruption is the romanticization of material poverty in certain progressive Christian traditions, in which the materially poor are treated as automatically spiritually privileged and the materially comfortable as automatically suspect, with material poverty itself elevated to a kind of virtue. This too is not the biblical doctrine. Material poverty is, in itself, a hardship and a burden that Scripture commands the church to relieve; it is not a virtue, and Scripture nowhere commends it as such. What Christ calls blessed is poverty of spirit—the inward state of bankruptcy before God that casts itself entirely upon the grace of Christ—a state to which the materially poor may have easier access (because their condition has not insulated them against the gospel’s diagnosis) but to which the materially comfortable can equally come if they will hear the diagnosis Revelation 3 makes of the Laodicean condition. Recover both ends. The materially poor are to be relieved; the spiritually poor are to be blessed; the materially rich are warned against the dangers their wealth poses to their souls; and all alike, rich and poor, are called to the poverty of spirit that alone can receive the riches of Christ—the Christ who Himself became poor that all might be made rich in Him.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew rīsh / rēsh (poverty) and ‘ānī (poor, afflicted); Greek ptōcheia (destitution) and ptōchos (the begging poor)—both the material poverty Scripture commands the church to relieve and the poverty of spirit Christ pronounces blessed at the gate of His kingdom.

expand to see more

Greek ptōchos (G4434) — poor, beggar, destitute (the “poor in spirit” of Matt 5:3).

Greek ptōcheia (G4432) — poverty, destitution (2 Cor 8:2, 9).

Hebrew rīsh / rēsh (H7389) — poverty, want.

Hebrew ‘ānī (H6041) — poor, afflicted, humble (often used of the spiritually poor in the Psalter).

Usage

"Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven—the opening Beatitude diagnoses the inward state of bankruptcy that alone can receive the riches of Christ."

"Though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich—the divine emptying that became the church’s eternal riches."

"Prosperity gospel reads wealth as God’s favor; progressive romanticization reads poverty as virtue; biblical doctrine refuses both and holds material and spiritual poverty in their proper distinct registers."
